tracks.title: Toledo in five minutes: the city on the rock

sections.title: The city that translated the world

segments.text: Welcome to Toledo, Monica.
Before any church or painting, here is the story of the city itself.
It takes five minutes, and everything else today will make more sense.
Start with the ground under your feet.
Toledo sits on a hill of granite, and the river Tagus wraps around it on three sides, in a deep gorge.
Only one side is open.
Whoever held this rock was very hard to remove.
So everyone wanted it.
The Romans took it first, about two hundred years before Christ.
One of their historians called it a small city, but strong because of its position.
They built baths, a circus for chariot races, and the water tanks you can still visit underground.
When Rome collapsed, a people from the north moved in.
The Visigoths.
They made Toledo the capital of all Spain.
Their kings were crowned here, and their bishops met here to decide what the country would believe.
Remember them.
Their last king, Rodrigo, is waiting for you in tonight's legends.
Then, in seven hundred and eleven, an army crossed from Africa.
Within a few years, Toledo was a Muslim city, and it stayed one for nearly four hundred years.
The narrow twisting lanes you keep getting lost in are their street plan.
The little mosque by the city gate is theirs.
You have just come from Granada, the last Muslim kingdom in Spain.
Granada fell in fourteen ninety-two.
Toledo was taken by a Christian king four centuries earlier, in ten eighty-five.
It was the first great Muslim city to fall.
And that is the reason it matters so much.
Because the new Christian king did something unusual.
He did not empty the city.
Muslims stayed.
Jews stayed.
And so did their libraries.
Those libraries held books Europe had lost.
Greek medicine, astronomy, mathematics, Aristotle.
All of it kept alive in Arabic.
So scholars came to Toledo from England, Italy and Germany, and sat down with Jewish and Muslim translators.
A book would go from Arabic into Spanish, spoken aloud, and from Spanish into Latin, written down.
Think about that, with your own story.
Knowledge passing from one language to the next, across a table, between people who prayed differently.
Much of what Europe later called its Renaissance came through rooms in this town.
It was not paradise.
There were taxes, quarrels, and massacres.
But for a few centuries, three faiths shared this small rock, and built in each other's styles.
You will see churches that look like mosques, built by Muslim craftsmen for Christian priests.
It ended badly.
In fourteen ninety-two, the Jews of Spain were told to convert or leave.
Ten years later, the Muslims were told the same.
The city of three faiths became a city of one.
For a while Toledo was still the heart of an empire.
The emperor Charles the Fifth, the one you saw on horseback in the Prado, held court here.
Then his son moved the capital to a small town in the middle of nowhere, called Madrid.
The court left.
The money left.
And Toledo simply stopped.
Nobody could afford to knock it down and build it again.
That is why you are walking through a medieval city today.
It was preserved by being forgotten.
One man arrived a few years after the court had gone.
A painter from Greece, hoping to work for the king.
The king tried him once, and did not like the result.
So he stayed here for the rest of his life, and painted this city's priests, its noblemen and its stormy sky.
You know him already.
El Greco.
That is Toledo.
Romans, Goths, Muslims, Christians and Jews, all on one rock, and then four centuries of sleep.
Now choose your next track.
The cathedral, Santo Tomé, or whatever is in front of you.

tracks.room: Anywhere. Listen first.

tracks.title: The day the inquisitors came

sections.title: A room full of silent things

segments.text: Monica, this one is for the room that let you down.
You went down the steps.
There was a rack.
A chair of spikes.
Iron collars behind glass.
Little cards with a name and a date.
And you walked out thinking, is that it?
It was not your fault.
Objects cannot speak.
A rope on a wall is only a rope until you know whose arms it held, and why, and what the people in the room were writing down while it happened.
So let me give the objects back their people.
Real people, of this city.
Some of their words survive, written by a clerk with a quill, in the very hours they spoke them.
But first, a question to carry with you.
Why here?
Why did Toledo, of all the cities in Spain, become one of the great homes of the Spanish Inquisition?
Picture Toledo a few years before Columbus sails.
Church bells, and the call of the synagogue, and in living memory the call to prayer.
Christians, Jews and Muslims have shared these streets for centuries.
Not always kindly.
But they have shared them.
And there is a fourth group, the one that matters most to our story.
The conversos.
Jewish families who became Christian, many of them after terrible riots a century earlier, when converting was the price of staying alive.
Their grandchildren are Christians born and baptised.
Some are priests.
Some are rich.
Some sit on the city council.
And their neighbours do not trust them.
Toledo has already passed one of the first laws in Spain to bar people of Jewish descent from office.
The question in every whisper is simple.
Do they still keep the old faith in secret, behind closed shutters, on a Friday night?
Now the inquisitors arrive.
It is the spring of fourteen eighty-five.
They come from a smaller town to the south, and in the cathedral one of them preaches a sermon announcing their powers.
Then they post an edict on the cathedral door.
It is called the edict of grace.
Anyone who has strayed from the faith has forty days to come forward and confess.
Confess now, and you will be treated with mercy.
In the city, they said there was a plot.
A group of conversos, it was told, planned to attack the Corpus Christi procession and kill the inquisitors.
Some men were hanged for it.
Whether the plot was real, historians still argue.
Imagine being a converso family that spring.
Do you confess, even if you have nothing to confess, just to be safe?
And if you do, which of your neighbours will you be asked to name?
The following February, on a cold Sunday morning, the first great ceremony takes place.
About seven hundred and fifty people walk through these streets in procession.
Men and women from seven parishes.
Bareheaded.
Barefoot in the cold.
Each carries an unlit candle.
Crowds come from the countryside to watch.
They are not burned.
They are the ones who confessed.
Their punishment is shame, fines, and a life marked forever.
A chronicler of the day wrote it all down.
And this was only the beginning.
Hold that image.
Seven hundred and fifty candles, none of them lit.
Next, one woman, one accusation, and the words she spoke in a room very like the one you saw today.

tracks.room: Anywhere

tracks.title: Stop 1. Elvira del Campo: the woman who would not eat pork

segments.text: A summer day, in a village south of Toledo.
A notary's wife is arrested and brought to the city.
Her name is Elvira del Campo.
She is pregnant.
She is a Christian, baptised, a churchgoer.
But her family were Jewish, generations ago.
The charge?
Two men who lived in her own house have spoken to the Inquisition.
They say she does not eat pork.
And that she puts on clean linen on Saturdays, the Jewish sabbath.
That is all.
A plate pushed away.
A fresh shirt on the wrong day.
Now here is the first thing that makes this court so frightening.
Elvira is never told who accused her.
She is not told exactly what they said, or when.
She has to guess.
So she guesses.
She lists everyone she thinks might hate her.
Twelve names.
The judges agree to strike out two.
One of them, it turns out, had a grudge against her.
And she fights back.
Thirteen witnesses come to speak for her.
A good Christian, they say, every one of them but one.
Why no pork?
Elvira says a doctor told her to avoid it, for an illness she was ashamed of.
Months pass in her cell.
Her baby is born there.
Then the judges vote.
The case is not proven.
So they order the question, which is what they called torture.
She is taken to the chamber.
In the room are an inquisitor, a representative of the bishop, a doctor, and a clerk.
The clerk has one job.
To write down every word she says.
Because of him, we can still hear her.
She is told to tell the truth.
She says she has nothing to tell.
The cords are tied to her arms, and tightened, turn by turn.
And between each turn, she begs.
Not for mercy, at first.
For instructions.
Tell me what you want, for I do not know what to say.
Again and again.
Tell me what I have to say.
She cannot give them what they want, because no one will tell her what it is.
That is the rule.
The court must never put words in the prisoner's mouth.
That first day, she confesses nothing.
Four days later she is brought back to the room.
And before the cords are touched, she breaks.
Yes, she says.
When I was a girl, my mother told me not to eat pork, and to keep the sabbath.
The next day, outside the chamber, she repeats it, as the rules demand.
In June of fifteen sixty-eight, she walks in a great public ceremony in Toledo.
She is reconciled, as they called it.
Taken back into the Church.
Her property is confiscated.
She must wear a penitent's yellow tunic, and serve three years in prison.
After six months the prison term is lifted.
She walks out free, and with nothing.
The record says she was reduced to begging.
Her file is still in Spain's national archive in Madrid.
Hundreds of pages.
A woman who could not read, and whose every cry was written down.
Ask yourself what you would have said.
Tell me what I have to say.
Next, the ceremony she walked in, and the square where Toledo staged the greatest of them.
You have stood in it.

tracks.room: Anywhere

tracks.title: Stop 2. Zocodover: the theatre of faith

segments.text: If you can, stand in Zocodover, the big three-sided square at the top of the town.
Cafés.
Pigeons.
A tourist train.
Now take all of that away.
It is February, fifteen sixty.
The king of Spain, Philip the Second, has just married a French princess.
She is fourteen years old.
And Toledo wants to give the royal couple a spectacle worthy of them.
For its greatest ceremonies, Toledo built a stage in this square.
Picture it now.
Wooden stands rise against the houses.
Balconies are rented out like boxes at the opera.
There is a raised platform for the inquisitors, under a canopy, and another for the accused.
The king and his young queen come to watch.
What Toledo offers them is an auto-da-fé.
An act of faith.
The words sound like fire.
But here is the surprise.
An auto-da-fé was not a burning.
It was a ceremony of sentences.
A mass, a sermon, and then, one by one, the verdicts read aloud.
It begins at dawn with a procession.
A green cross, the emblem of the Inquisition, carried through the streets.
Then the accused, walking in file, each with a candle.
Watch their clothes.
That is how the crowd knew everything.
Many wear a yellow tunic with a red diagonal cross.
That is the sanbenito.
It means: I confessed, I was taken back, I am being punished and forgiven.
Elvira del Campo wore one.
A few wear something darker.
A tall pointed hat.
A tunic painted with flames and devils.
Those are the ones who will not be forgiven.
The sentences take hours.
Most people are given penance.
Prayer, fines, years of the yellow tunic, sometimes the lash, sometimes the galleys.
A great many walk home that night.
And the ones in flames?
The Church did not execute them itself.
It released them, that was the word, into the hands of the royal courts.
They were led out of the city, down to the open fields of the Vega, below the walls.
There, at a place Toledo called the brasero, the brazier, the sentence was carried out.
Those who repented at the end were strangled first.
Not in this square.
The square was for the theatre.
The fire was out of sight.
Here is the cruellest part, and the least known.
When a penitent's years were done, the yellow tunic was not thrown away.
It was hung on the wall of their parish church.
With their name on it.
Their children saw it every Sunday.
Their grandchildren too.
When the cloth rotted, the Inquisition had it replaced, with the same name, so that the shame would never fade.
Families were refused marriages, offices, honours, for generations, because of a tunic on a wall.
How many died?
Fewer than the legend says, and more than anyone should accept.
Modern historians, counting the trial records, find that from fifteen forty onwards, fewer than two in every hundred people tried were executed.
The worst killing came in the first fifty years.
Across Spain and its whole history, the best estimates are a few thousand.
Look around the square.
Picture the stands, the canopy, a fourteen-year-old queen watching.
Next, the instruments.
Which of the things in those glass cases are real, and which were made to frighten you.

tracks.room: Plaza de Zocodover, or anywhere

tracks.title: Stop 3. The instruments: what was real, and what was made to frighten

sections.title: The ones that were real, elsewhere
The one that was all too real

segments.text: Here is a fact that surprises almost everyone.
The Spanish Inquisition used only three methods of torture.
Three.
The first is the pulley.
In Spanish, the garrucha.
A rope tied to the wrists, behind the back, and the prisoner lifted from the floor.
The second is the water.
The toca, a strip of linen in the mouth, and water poured onto it from a jar, a little at a time.
The third is the rack.
The potro, a frame where cords were tightened around the arms and legs.
A wooden frame like a ladder, a pulley with a rope, a jar and a cloth.
Those are the ones to trust.
And they came with a rulebook.
Torture only at the end of a long trial, never at the start.
A doctor in the room.
A clerk writing every word.
No blood to be shed.
Only once, in theory, though a session could be suspended.
And a confession made in pain counted for nothing until the prisoner repeated it, a day later, away from the ropes.
In this city, a historian studied over a thousand trials from around the year sixteen hundred.
About one prisoner in eight was tortured.
The royal courts of the day were often harsher.
That is not a comfort.
It is a measure of the age.
Now the famous pieces.
The iron maiden.
A tall iron woman, hinged, full of spikes.
Did anyone ever die in one?
Almost certainly not.
No record from the Middle Ages mentions it.
The first story appears in a German city guidebook at the end of the seventeen hundreds.
Showmen then built them for display and sold them to collectors.
The most famous was destroyed in the Second World War, long known to be a fake.
The pear of anguish, the metal pear that opens with a screw?
No sign of one as a torture tool before the eighteen hundreds.
The chastity belt?
Medieval writers mention it mostly as a joke.
Most surviving belts are later curiosities.
The Judas cradle, the pointed seat?
The evidence is thin and late.
Some pieces are real, but not the Inquisition's.
Masks of shame, iron faces with long ears or a pig's snout, were worn by gossips and cheats in German towns.
Boots that crushed the legs were used by courts in Scotland and France.
So who made all this?
Some were forged for money, then gathered by collectors, and from the nineteen eighties sent around Europe in touring shows.
Why did they settle so happily in Spain?
Because people had been told for centuries that Spain was the land of horrors.
Protestant pamphlets, in the age of the wars of religion, painted the Inquisition as a cave of monsters.
Then, in the eighteen forties, an American writer set his most famous terror tale in the dungeons of Toledo.
A pit, a swinging blade.
Pure invention.
Spanish historians later gave this a name.
The Black Legend.
The truth was bad enough.
The legend made it worse.
Now find the garrote, if they have one.
A chair, a post, an iron collar with a screw at the back.
This one is real.
Spain made it the official means of execution in the eighteen thirties.
The last man put to death for heresy in Spain was a village schoolteacher near Valencia, garroted in eighteen twenty-six, because he would not teach his pupils the Catholic faith.
And the last two garrotings in Spain took place in March, nineteen seventy-four.
One in Barcelona, one in Tarragona.
Within living memory.
Stand with that for a moment.
Last, the cells.
Where prisoners actually waited, and what we should take away with us.

tracks.title: Stop 4. The cells: the brotherhood's prison, and what remains

segments.text: Near the cathedral, in a narrow street, there is an old stone doorway.
Look up at it.
Above the door, the arms of the Catholic Monarchs.
And on either side, two small armed guards with crossbows.
This was the house of the Holy Brotherhood.
Not the Inquisition.
Something older, and in its way more feared on a lonely road.
Long before the inquisitors came, the hills south of Toledo were wild country.
Beekeepers, hunters and shepherds lived out there, and so did bandits.
So the country people banded together into an armed brotherhood, to hunt the robbers down themselves.
Later the Catholic Monarchs took the idea across all of Castile.
A rural police, with its own judges and its own jails.
People mocked them, too.
Their uniform had green sleeves.
And when help came too late, Spaniards would say: at a fine hour, green sleeves.
They still say it today.
In Don Quixote, after the knight frees a chain of convicts, his squire Sancho is terrified of one thing.
Not the convicts.
The Holy Brotherhood, coming after them.
If the lower floor is open, go down.
The cells are underground, vaulted rooms with iron bars, gathered around a shaft that drops daylight from the street above.
Each room, it is said, could hold up to forty prisoners.
Stand by the bars and look up at that light.
That pale square is all a prisoner had of the day.
It is the most honest thing in the building.
No label needed.
And the Inquisition's own cells?
They were called the secret prisons.
In Toledo, for more than two centuries, the tribunal had its house beside the church of San Vicente, in the upper town.
Nothing of them is open to visit today.
Here is a twist the legend never tells.
The Inquisition's cells were often cleaner and better fed than the king's jails.
Historians have found prisoners in the king's jails who blasphemed on purpose, just to be moved into them.
But they were secret in a way no ordinary jail was.
You did not know why you were there.
You could not see your family.
You might wait months or years, as Elvira del Campo waited, guessing at your accusers in the dark.
In Toledo, people say tunnels ran from the Inquisition's house under the streets, to the cathedral and beyond.
Guides will point to cellars and swear by them.
No one has ever shown such a tunnel to be real.
But the city loves the story.
The tribunal of Toledo sat for the last time in eighteen twenty, and the Inquisition was abolished for good in eighteen thirty-four.
Its papers went to Madrid.
Thousands of trials.
Names, recipes, prayers, the gossip of kitchens, the cries in the chamber, all written down.
That is the strange gift of this cruel court.
It kept such careful records that the people it tried to erase are still here.
We know what Elvira del Campo ate, and what she wore on a Saturday, and what she said when her arms hurt.
So if you walk past a glass case again, Monica, look for the plain things.
A rope.
A jar.
A yellow tunic.
And put a person beside each one.
Not monsters, on either side.
A city that let fear of its neighbours become law.
That is the darkest thing in Toledo, and it was never kept in a dungeon.
Walk up into the light.
Toledo is still the city of three faiths, in its stones.
Thank you for listening.

tracks.room: Posada de la Hermandad, Calle de la Hermandad, near the cathedral, or anywhere

tracks.title: Stop 0. The Cathedral: A broken promise

sections.title: Two and a half centuries of stone

segments.text: Welcome, Monica.
Play this outside, before you go in, or while you wait in the queue at the Puerta Llana, the plain door on the side street.
It is the only door of this cathedral with no steps up to it.
Picture this spot nine hundred and forty years ago.
No Gothic towers.
A great mosque, the main mosque of a Muslim city.
And before the mosque, people said, a Visigothic church.
The ground under your feet has changed faith twice.
Then a Christian king, Alfonso the Sixth of Castile, takes Toledo.
The city surrenders on terms.
One of the terms is a promise.
The Muslims of Toledo will keep their great mosque.
It lasted about a year.
The king rides out of the city.
Behind him stay two people who never liked that promise.
His French queen, Constance.
And the new archbishop, Bernard, a monk from the great abbey of Cluny in Burgundy.
While the king is away, they send armed men into the mosque.
They set up an altar.
They hang a bell in the minaret.
The mosque is a church.
The king hears, and he is furious.
One later chronicler says he swore to put the guilty to death.
Now the legend.
The Muslims of Toledo, it is said, sent their wisest man, a jurist named Abu Walid, to meet the angry king.
And the jurist begged him to forgive.
Let it stand, he said.
Do not shed blood for our mosque.
The king's anger cooled.
And the cathedral never forgot.
Inside, on a pillar of the main chapel, they say a carved figure honours that Muslim peacemaker.
That is legend; no document proves it.
You will meet him later.
The old mosque served as cathedral for well over a hundred years.
Then, in twelve twenty-six, a king laid the first stone of this one.
It took over two and a half centuries.
If you walked past the main front, in the square, you saw it.
Two towers were planned.
Only one was ever finished.
The other stops short and wears a small dome, like a hat.
The archbishops of Toledo were the richest churchmen in Spain.
Almost everything inside was paid for by such men, and every one wanted to be remembered.
Nine stops follow, in the order you will walk, with a short goodbye at the end.
Each stop tells you where to go.
When you hear a pause, stop the track, look, then play on.
Things get moved.
If something is not where I say, check the floor plan.
The bell tower climb may need its own ticket or a time slot.
Ask at the ticket shop before you go in.
If you only have thirty minutes, do these five.
The war carved in wood around the choir.
The hole in the roof behind the high altar.
The painted ceiling of the chapter house.
El Greco's red robe in the sacristy.
And the tower of silver in the treasury.
Now go in through the Puerta Llana.
Once inside, look along the walls near the door for a painted giant.
When you find him, play stop one.

tracks.room: Outside, by the Puerta Llana on Calle Cardenal Cisneros

tracks.title: Stop 1. The Nave: A giant, a stone, and a book that would not burn

sections.title: The man who keeps you alive today
The night the Virgin came down
The book that would not burn

segments.text: Stop one.
You are just inside.
Somewhere on the wall near the Lions' Door, the great carved door at the end of the cross aisle, there is a painted man as tall as a house.
A giant wading through water with a child on his shoulder.
Find him.
Saint Christopher, the ferryman who carried the Christ child across a river.
Why so big?
Because of a belief.
In the Middle Ages, people said that if you looked at Saint Christopher, you would not die a sudden death that day.
So churches painted him huge, by the doors.
You have just looked.
You are safe until midnight.
Now walk west along the nave, toward the main doors, under the forest of pillars.
Look for a small chapel built between two pillars, standing almost free in the aisle, with a little roof of carved stone.
Check the floor plan if you cannot see it.
Thirteen centuries ago, the archbishop of this city was a scholar named Ildefonsus.
He wrote a fierce book in honour of the Virgin Mary.
And this is what Toledo tells.
One night, before dawn, he came into his church to sing the morning prayers.
The Virgin was seated on his chair, surrounded by angels.
She thanked him for his book, and laid on his shoulders a robe made in heaven.
That is legend.
This chapel stands where the altar of the old Visigothic church is believed to have stood.
Behind its grille the cathedral keeps a stone.
The stone, they say, on which the Virgin set her feet.
Find it through the grille.
A plain piece of rock, in a building of gold.
Now carry on to the far corner, by the main doors, under the tower that was never finished.
It may be open only for its morning service; look through the bars.
For nearly four hundred years Toledo was a Muslim city.
Its Christians stayed, and kept praying in their own old way, in the words of the Visigoths.
They were called Mozarabs.
Then a Christian king took the city, and Rome wanted that old rite gone.
The legend says Toledo fought back.
First, a duel.
Two knights, one for the old rite, one for the Roman.
The Toledan knight won.
The king was not satisfied.
So, a trial by fire.
Both prayer books thrown on a bonfire.
And the old Toledan book would not burn.
But the king chose Rome anyway.
They say that is where Spaniards got an old proverb.
Laws go where kings want.
The legend is a later story.
What is true is this.
The old rite did not die.
A few parishes kept it, barely.
Four centuries later, Cardinal Cisneros, the hard, ascetic friar who ran Spain for Queen Isabella, had its books printed and built this chapel for it.
Its mass is still said here every morning.
If you can see the walls, look for battle paintings.
The conquest of Oran, in North Africa, a war Cisneros led himself, an old friar riding with the army.
A way of praying older than this building, kept alive inside it.
Walk on.
Go to the opposite corner of the church, under the finished tower, to the treasury chapel.
Play stop two.

tracks.room: South aisle by the entrance, then west along the nave to the Mozarabic chapel

tracks.title: Stop 2. The Treasury: The queen's jewel inside the tower of silver

segments.text: Stop two.
The treasury chapel, at the foot of the tower.
In the middle, behind glass, a tower of silver taller than a man.
Walk all the way round it before you listen on.
Begin with a death.
Queen Isabella dies, and she has left orders.
Her debts must be paid and her promises kept, so her possessions go up for sale.
The private treasures of the most powerful woman in Europe.
Among them is a small monstrance.
A case of gold to hold the holy bread of the Mass, so that people can see it carried before them.
It had been made for her, by a goldsmith in Barcelona.
The canons of this cathedral buy it.
And then the man who had been her confessor, Cardinal Cisneros, the friar you met in the last stop, has an idea.
He wants a setting for the queen's jewel.
Not a box.
A building.
He hires a German goldsmith living in Spain, Enrique de Arfe.
Arfe works on it for seven years.
Look at it now as Arfe meant it.
It is a Gothic church in miniature.
Buttresses, pinnacles, pointed arches, a spire.
On it, they say, about two hundred and sixty tiny figures.
Find the heart of it.
Behind the glass, in the middle of the silver tower, a smaller piece, golden.
That is Isabella's monstrance.
The queen's private piece, swallowed by a cathedral.
Now the tradition.
The guides of Toledo love to say that the gold of this inner piece came from the first gold Columbus brought back from the Americas, and that the queen gave it for this.
Nobody has proved it.
But stand here and think about it.
Gold from a world the queen had never seen, melted down to hold a scrap of bread.
Once a year, at the feast of Corpus Christi, it comes out of this room.
It is lifted onto a carriage and taken through the streets of Toledo, under awnings hung across the narrow lanes against the sun.
It has made that journey for about five hundred years.
Arfe left it in silver.
Later generations, it is said, gilded it and set it on a grander base.
Everyone who looked after it wanted his share in it.
Look around the room for books in cases.
If it is on show, one of them is a great treasure of the Middle Ages: a Bible in three volumes made in Paris for the French king Louis the Ninth, the crusader who became a saint.
Thousands of tiny painted pictures.
How it came to Toledo is not certain; the stories differ.
A saint king.
A queen who backed Columbus.
A goldsmith from Germany.
All gathered in one small room, because a frugal friar wanted the holy bread to ride through the streets in a cathedral of its own.
Walk on.
Go back toward the centre of the church, to the great enclosed choir in the middle of the nave.
Find the way in, on the side that faces the high altar.
Play stop three.

tracks.room: Treasury chapel, at the foot of the bell tower, near the main doors

tracks.title: Stop 3. The Choir: A war carved while it was still being fought

segments.text: Stop three.
The choir, the walled room in the middle of the nave where the canons sang.
Step in.
Two rows of wooden seats run round you, one high, one low.
Go close to the lower row, and look at the carved panels above the backs of the seats, at about the height of your chest.
Picture a workshop in Toledo.
A German woodcarver, Rodrigo Alemán, has just been given a strange order by the canons.
Carve the war.
The war is the war of Granada.
The last Muslim kingdom in Spain.
Isabella and Ferdinand are taking it town by town, castle by castle.
And it is not over.
When the carver starts, the Alhambra is still Muslim.
News comes in.
Another town has fallen.
A new panel is begun.
Fifty-four panels.
Most of them, a historian worked out, can be matched to a real town or castle, often by a name carved on them.
Look closely at one.
Walls and towers like a child's castle.
Ladders.
Knights in armour, with banners.
And on the walls, the defenders in turbans.
Look for a gate opening.
A surrender.
Now find a face on the losing side.
You have walked through the Alhambra.
These are the people who lost it.
Imagine one of them about to give up the city where his grandparents are buried.
Now look down, under the seats.
Folded up, each seat shows a small ledge, so an old canon could lean while seeming to stand.
On these ledges and on the armrests, look for animals, monsters, odd little faces.
Rodrigo Alemán had a name for mischief.
In another cathedral, at Plasencia, his carvings under the seats are famous for being rude.
And Plasencia tells a legend about him.
That he was shut up in a tower, built himself wings, and jumped.
It is only a story.
Now look up at the high row of seats, behind and above you.
A generation later, another archbishop wanted the upper stalls.
He did not hire one master.
He hired two, and gave each one half.
On one side, Felipe Bigarny, from Burgundy, the old master.
On the other, Alonso Berruguete, a Spaniard who had been to Italy as a young man, and had seen Michelangelo at work.
The old style against the new.
Compare the two sides.
Bigarny's figures are calm, balanced.
Berruguete's twist and strain, as if the wood could not hold them.
Which side is whose?
Look at which side makes you nervous.
That is Berruguete.
The old master died before the work was done.
At the far end, the archbishop's throne, and above it Berruguete's Transfiguration, Christ rising in light.
He took the place of honour.
Last, look for a stone statue of the Virgin and Child, painted white, standing on the altar inside the choir.
Look at the mother, then at the child.
Their faces turn to each other.
Is she smiling?
Decide for yourself.
She was already famous in the fourteenth century, more than a hundred years before the war around her was carved.
A mother and a baby, in the middle of a war.
Walk on.
Leave the choir and cross to the high altar, behind the tall iron grille.
Play stop four.

tracks.room: The choir, enclosed in the middle of the nave

tracks.title: Stop 4. The Main Chapel: The third king of Spain

sections.title: The cardinal who would not lie in a side chapel

segments.text: Stop four.
Stand at the great grille of the high altar, with your back to the choir.
Look.
A wall of carved and gilded wood, rising almost to the vault.
Hundreds of figures, set in rows like the windows of a building.
It tells the life of Christ, from the bottom up, and at the very top, under a painted sky of stars, the crucifixion.
It was built about five hundred years ago, for Cardinal Cisneros, the friar you have already met twice.
To make room for something this big, the chapel itself had to be enlarged, and the tombs of old kings had to be moved.
Look up at the top of the grille in front of you.
The double-headed eagle of the emperor Charles the Fifth.
If you saw Titian's Charles on horseback in the Prado, this is his badge, in iron.
Now look to your left, inside the chapel, in the side wall.
A tomb of white marble, shaped like a Roman triumphal arch.
This is the tomb of Cardinal Pedro González de Mendoza.
In his day, people called him the third king of Spain.
He was Isabella's closest adviser.
They say that when Granada fell, it was the cardinal's silver cross that was raised first on the towers of the Alhambra.
It is a story told about that day.
He also had sons.
A cardinal, with children, and nobody pretended otherwise.
Isabella, it is reported, called them the cardinal's three beautiful sins.
Now the fight.
Mendoza wanted to be buried here, in the main chapel, beside the kings.
The canons of the cathedral said no.
This was the place of kings.
Then the queen stepped in.
She and the archbishop overruled the chapter.
The old wall was broken through to make space for him.
And look at the style.
Not Gothic.
A classical arch, straight out of Renaissance Italy, one of the first in all of Castile.
Even in death, the cardinal arrived first.
Toledo tells it with more drama.
They say the canons would not give way, so the queen had the wall knocked through at night, while they slept, and by morning it was done.
No document records it.
But it is the version the city prefers.
Now look at the pillars that frame the chapel, at the edges of the grille.
Among the stone figures high up, two do not belong to any Bible story.
Check the floor plan if you cannot find them.
On one side, a figure Toledo calls the alfaquí, the jurist.
Tradition says this is Abu Walid, the Muslim jurist from the opening track, who begged the king to spare the men who seized his mosque.
His people lost their mosque, and he is honoured inside it.
On another pillar, a shepherd.
Toledo calls him Martín Alhaja.
The legend says that before the great battle of Las Navas de Tolosa, when a Christian army was trapped in the mountains, a shepherd appeared and showed the king a secret pass.
The army got through and won.
Both are legends.
But think about who is up there.
The kings lie below.
On the pillars, a Muslim peacemaker and a shepherd from the hills.
Walk on.
Go round the right-hand side of the main chapel into the curved walkway behind it, the ambulatory.
On your right, look for a doorway into a hall, the chapter house.
Play stop five.

tracks.room: Capilla Mayor, the high altar, seen through the grille facing the choir

tracks.title: Stop 5. The Chapter House: A room that watches you decide

sections.title: The men who ran the money

segments.text: Stop five.
The chapter house.
You enter through a small antechamber, then the hall.
Before anything else, stop in the doorway of the hall and look up.
A ceiling of carved wood, gold and colour, set in deep boxes, like the inside of a jewel case.
It was made by Toledan carpenters in the Mudéjar way, the craft Christian Spain learned from its Muslim builders, the craft of the Alhambra ceilings.
And it was made only a few years after Granada fell.
This is where the canons met.
The chapter.
Picture them, a few dozen men in black, seated on the benches round these walls.
They managed the income of the richest church in Spain.
They hired the painters and the carvers.
They argued with the archbishop.
You have already met them saying no, to a cardinal who wanted a tomb among the kings.
Now look at the walls above the benches.
Painted all over, by Juan de Borgoña, the leading painter of Toledo in Cisneros's day.
Scenes from the life of the Virgin.
Find the end wall.
The Last Judgement.
Souls rising from their graves.
Some lifted to heaven.
Some dragged down to hell.
Look at the faces of the damned.
Think about where it is.
Not in a chapel for the people.
In the boardroom.
Every time these men voted on money or on a fight with the archbishop, this was in front of them.
You will answer for what you decide in this room.
Now look lower, along the walls, under the paintings.
A long row of portraits, one after another, like a family album.
Every archbishop of Toledo, in order.
The oldest faces are invented.
Those men lived in Roman and Visigothic times, and nobody knew what they looked like.
Then, as you walk along, the faces become real people.
Look for one in particular.
A lean, old man, seen in profile, with a long nose and a hollow cheek, in a plain dark habit.
Cardinal Cisneros.
Check the names painted under the portraits.
This portrait is one of the few likenesses of him made in his lifetime.
A friar who walked barefoot, who slept on boards, they said, under his silk.
Who ran Spain twice as regent.
The man behind the gold altar, the silver tower, the old rite, and this room.
And he chose to paint himself into a line more than a thousand years long.
He was telling anyone who entered: I am not one man.
I am the latest in a chain that goes back to the saints.
Now go to the other end of the row.
The series has never stopped.
Each new archbishop has been added.
Find the last face on the wall.
Every archbishop who sits in this room knows that one day his own face will join the line.
Walk on.
Go back out into the ambulatory, and continue round behind the high altar.
Stop when the light changes, then turn and look up.
Play stop six.

tracks.room: Sala Capitular, off the right-hand side of the ambulatory

tracks.title: Stop 6. The Transparente: The archbishop who cut a hole in the roof

segments.text: Stop six.
You are in the walkway behind the high altar.
On one side, a wall of marble and bronze, swirling up toward the roof.
Do not look at it yet.
Look up first, at the vault above your head, on the opposite side.
There is a hole.
A great opening, cut through the stone vault of a Gothic cathedral, framed with painted clouds and figures.
Daylight pours through it.
Here is why.
On the other side of this wall, inside the high altar, the cathedral kept the holy bread of the Mass in its tabernacle.
And it sat in the dark, behind the huge gilded altarpiece you saw in stop four.
An archbishop, Diego de Astorga, wanted that to change.
He wanted light to fall on the holy bread, and he wanted people behind the altar to be able to see through to it.
Hence the name.
The Transparente.
The see-through.
He gave the job to the cathedral's architect, Narciso Tomé, a sculptor who worked with his sons.
They worked for years.
Then they did the thing no medieval builder would have dared.
They cut through the vault of the ambulatory and let the sky in.
Now turn and look at the marble.
Stand back.
Clouds of stone.
Angels tumbling down on rays of gilded bronze.
In the middle, an oval opening, the window to the tabernacle, ringed with angels.
Above it, find a table and figures around it.
The Last Supper, carved in marble, floating in mid air.
When it was unveiled, the city held festivities.
A poet called it the eighth wonder of the world.
It cost a fortune, two hundred thousand ducats, it is said.
Then taste changed.
Later critics, who loved the calm lines of ancient Greece and Rome, found it overloaded and theatrical.
People still argue.
Which are you?
Stand there a moment and decide.
The archbishop got what he wanted in one more way.
Look at the floor in front of it, or check the floor plan.
He is buried here, at the foot of his own work, under the light he let in.
Now look up again, into the vaults round about, and into the chapels opening off this walkway.
Look for something small and red, hanging on cords high above the floor.
A wide, flat hat with tassels.
These are cardinals' hats.
When a cardinal of Toledo was buried, his red hat was hung from the vault above his tomb.
And the guides of Toledo tell what happens next.
The hat stays there, gathering dust, rotting slowly.
And when at last it falls to the floor, they say, the cardinal's soul is free of purgatory, and goes up to heaven.
That is a saying, not doctrine.
Count how many hats are still hanging on.
Walk on round the ambulatory.
Just behind you is the central chapel of Saint Ildefonsus, with a cardinal's tomb in the middle.
Next to it, the chapel of Santiago, with two white tombs side by side.
Find that one.
Play stop seven.

tracks.room: Ambulatory, directly behind the high altar

tracks.title: Stop 7. The Chapel of Santiago: The favourite who lost his head

sections.title: The man who ruled the king

segments.text: Stop seven.
The chapel of Santiago.
Look through the grille.
In the middle, two tombs of white alabaster side by side.
A man in armour.
A woman beside him.
Both with their hands joined in prayer.
The man is Álvaro de Luna.
For three decades he was the most powerful man in Castile.
More powerful than the king.
He had come to court as a boy, and the boy king took to him.
The king made him Constable of Castile, then Master of the Order of Santiago, with its castles and its armies.
The great lords hated him for it.
Again and again they rose against him.
Again and again he won.
And he built this chapel as his own tomb, in the cathedral of the first city of Castile.
A grand chapel, with his family's crescent moons in the stone.
Look for them.
Now the legend.
On his first tomb here, they say, Don Álvaro placed a figure of himself in gilded bronze.
And it had a secret.
During Mass, by some hidden mechanism, the bronze man rose from his tomb, and knelt, and prayed.
That it moved is legend.
That there was a gilded bronze statue is recorded.
And its end is recorded too.
When his enemies took Toledo, they had it pulled down and melted.
When Don Álvaro heard, he is reported to have laughed.
There is no point, he said, in taking revenge on a statue.
The enemies would get the man himself instead.
In the end it was the queen.
The king's second wife distrusted the favourite, and she worked on her husband.
And one spring the king gave way.
The man who had ruled for him for thirty years was arrested, tried in haste, and condemned.
Picture the main square of Valladolid, an early summer day.
A scaffold.
He climbs it.
And afterwards his head is set high on a post and left there for days, for the crowd to see.
An old account adds one more thing.
His body lay on the scaffold beside a basin.
A basin for coins, collected from passers by, to pay for his burial.
The richest man in Castile, buried on charity.
And the queen who brought him down?
She was the mother of Isabella, then a baby of two.
The queen of the choir stalls and the silver tower.
His widow, Juana Pimentel, signed her letters after that as the sad countess.
She, and later their daughter, finished this chapel and brought him here.
The tombs you see were made decades after his death.
Look at the corners of the tombs.
Small kneeling figures keep watch, at his, knights of his order; at hers, friars.
And look at his face.
Calm, eyes closed, hands together.
No hint of the scaffold.
His family carved him the death he did not have.
Walk on round the ambulatory, past more chapels, toward the far side of the church.
Look for the large chapel of the New Kings, and beyond it the door of the sacristy.
Go into the sacristy.
Play stop eight.

tracks.room: Capilla de Santiago, off the ambulatory, beside the central chapel of Saint Ildefonsus

tracks.title: Stop 8. The Sacristy: El Greco against the cathedral

segments.text: Stop eight.
The sacristy.
A long, high hall hung with paintings.
Walk to the far end and stand before the painting on the end wall.
A man in a robe of blazing red, in a crowd of grey faces and steel.
Toledo, the late fifteen seventies.
A Greek painter in his thirties has just arrived from Italy.
Few in Spain know his name; they will soon call him simply the Greek.
Through a friend from Rome, the dean's son, he gets his first great Spanish commission.
A painting for this room.
Christ, about to be stripped of his clothes before the crucifixion.
He gives them this.
Look at the red.
It is the loudest colour in the cathedral.
Around him, helmets and faces pushing in.
Find the hands already reaching for the robe.
And at the lower right, find the man bent over, drilling holes in the cross, getting it ready.
The canons did not like it.
And when the time came to agree a price, they said so, in writing.
First, look at the heads.
The heads of the tormentors rise above the head of Christ.
Find them.
To the canons, that was an insult.
Nobody should stand higher than Christ.
Second, look at the lower left.
Three women.
The three Marys.
The canons pointed out, correctly, that the Gospel does not put them here at this moment.
Remove them, they said.
The painter's own expert valued the picture at nine hundred and fifty ducats.
The cathedral fought it.
He was awarded three hundred and fifty.
Little more than a third.
And the figures?
He was supposed to change them.
Look again at the three women and at the heads above Christ.
He never did.
They are still there.
A young foreigner, against the richest church in Spain.
He lost the money, and kept the painting exactly as he wanted it.
If you saw his saints in the Prado, this is where that Spanish story began.
Now turn round, and look up.
The ceiling is painted with a heaven full of figures, by Luca Giordano.
Find the scene in it.
The Virgin coming down to give Saint Ildefonsus his robe.
The legend from stop one.
Along the walls, look for a set of apostles, by the Greek again.
And look for Goya.
A dark, crowded Arrest of Christ, a crush of faces, from the painter of the Prado's black, haunted pictures.
There may be a Titian and a Caravaggio in the rooms beside; check the labels.
Beside the sacristy is the chapel of the Sagrario.
If you can see in, or check the floor plan, it holds the grave of Cardinal Portocarrero.
He stood by the bed of the last, sickly Habsburg king of Spain as he was dying without a child, and pressed him to leave his crown to a French prince.
The king did.
A war across Europe followed, for more than ten years.
And on his own gravestone, the cardinal ordered these words, in Latin.
Here lies dust, ashes, and nothing.
Walk on.
The last stop is the cloister.
The way in is on this side of the church, toward the bell tower; follow the signs, or check the floor plan.
Play stop nine.

tracks.room: Sacristy and picture gallery, off the left side of the ambulatory as you face the high altar

tracks.title: Stop 9. The Cloister and the Tower: A fire, and a bell that rang once

segments.text: Stop nine.
The cloister.
Step out into the arcades round the garden.
After the gold and the dark, open sky.
Before this cloister, there was no quiet here.
There was a market.
The alcaná, a tangle of shops and stalls pressed up against the cathedral, much of it run by Toledo's Jewish merchants.
Picture the cloth, the shouting, the noise.
Then came an archbishop who wanted the ground.
Pedro Tenorio.
A hard man, a builder of bridges.
He wanted a cloister worthy of his cathedral.
The market was in the way.
And here Toledo tells a dark story.
One night, it is said, the market caught fire.
The shops burned.
And with the market in ashes, the archbishop could buy the land.
Who started the fire?
The legend says it was set on purpose, to clear the way for him.
Nobody has ever proved it.
What is recorded is that work on this cloister began in the late thirteen eighties, on the ground where the market had been.
Two years later, in thirteen ninety-one, mobs attacked the Jewish quarters of Castile, Toledo among them.
The quiet arcades you are standing in were built in that decade.
Look at the walls now.
Large painted scenes, made centuries later, of Toledo's own saints and their lives.
Find the one that catches you.
Now look up, over the roofs, at the one finished tower of the cathedral.
If your ticket includes the climb, ask the staff where it starts; it may be by time slot.
About three hundred steps, a spiral, up to the clock and the bells.
Up there hangs the biggest of them all.
Toledo calls her la Gorda.
The fat one.
She weighs more than seventeen tonnes, and is nearly three and a half metres across.
In her day, one of the largest bells in Europe.
She was cast in the seventeen fifties.
Imagine the city waiting for her voice.
Then, the first time she was rung, she cracked.
People blamed the clapper.
Too big, they said, too heavy, swung too hard.
Others blamed a flaw in the casting.
What is certain is that she has been silent ever since.
The largest voice in Toledo, and it spoke once.
If you go up, look down on the city from beside her.
The river looping round the rock.
The churches you have walked to today.
And beneath you, this whole stone ship, built over a mosque, built over a church.
If you do not go up, stand in the garden and look at the tower.
Somewhere near the top, behind the openings, the fat lady is hanging in the dark, cracked and silent.
When you are ready, play the closing track, stop ten, here in the cloister or wherever you are.

tracks.room: Lower cloister, on the north side; bell tower if your ticket includes it

tracks.title: Stop 10. Goodbye: Everyone wanted to be remembered

segments.text: Stop ten, the last.
Sit, if you can.
Or step outside and look back at the tower.
Think of the people you met today.
Not the saints.
The people.
A queen and a monk who broke a king's promise while he was away.
A Muslim jurist who begged for peace, and was given a place on a pillar inside the mosque he lost.
A German carver who cut a war into walnut while the war was still being fought.
A cardinal who wanted to lie among kings, and a queen who knocked down a wall for him.
A friar who slept on boards and built in gold.
A favourite who ruled a king for decades, and was buried with coins from a basin.
A young Greek who lost his fee, and kept his three women in the picture.
And an archbishop who cut a hole in the roof to let the sun in.
Almost all of them wanted the same thing.
To be remembered.
They put their faces in the chapter house, their arms on the grilles, their bodies in the best places they could buy or fight for.
Only one of them, the man under the stone that says dust, ashes, and nothing, pretended not to care.
And even he made sure the words were carved.
Here is the question to take out with you.
Of everything in this building, what will you remember?
A gold altar?
A bell that rang once?
Or one face, in wood, on the walls of a town about to fall?
Monica, you have walked through the Alhambra, the prize at the end of the war in the choir.
You stood in front of El Greco in Madrid.
And today you have seen where his Spanish story started, with a quarrel over a red robe.
Thank you for walking it with me, all the way.
When you leave, go out the way the signs show you.
Step into the street, and look up one last time at the single tower.
The other one was never built.
The cathedral is still, in its way, unfinished.
Goodbye.

tracks.room: Anywhere; the cloister garden is a good place

tracks.title: Stop 1. Santo Tomé: The Burial of the Count of Orgaz

sections.title: A debt two hundred years old

segments.text: Stop one.
The church of Santo Tomé, with its brick tower.
The painting has its own entrance beside the church; check at the door.
Go in and stand back from it.
It fills the wall.
This picture starts with money.
A rich nobleman of Toledo, the lord of the town of Orgaz, loved this little parish church.
When he died, in thirteen twenty-three, he left it a gift to be paid every year, from Orgaz, for ever.
For ever lasted about two centuries.
Then the payments stopped.
The parish priest of Santo Tomé, Andrés Núñez, went to law.
He won.
And then he did something clever.
He decided the whole city should see, every day, why that money was owed.
He would put the nobleman's funeral on the wall, miracle and all.
So he hired the foreigner Toledo was talking about.
A painter from Crete.
They called him the Greek.
El Greco.
Here is the legend, as Toledo tells it.
At the funeral, as the body was about to be lowered, two saints came down from heaven.
Saint Stephen, young.
Saint Augustine, old and bearded.
They lifted the dead man with their own hands and laid him in his tomb, while the mourners stared.
That is legend.
The contract spelled it out: the miracle, the saints, and the crowd who saw it.
The painter would pay for his own materials.
The price would be set by valuers when it was done.
Look at the bottom half.
The two saints in gold, bending under the weight of a body in black armour.
How gently they hold him.
The old saint cradles his shoulders.
The young one holds his legs.
Now look closely at the young saint's robe, low down near his hem.
There is a tiny picture painted on it.
A man being stoned.
That is Stephen's own death, the first Christian martyr, embroidered on the clothes he wears to bury someone else.
Look at the row of men behind.
Black clothes.
White ruffs.
Long pale faces.
They look like portraits because many of them were.
Gentlemen of Toledo in El Greco's own day, not the dead man's.
The painter put his neighbours at a funeral two hundred and sixty years old.
On the right, in a white robe, reading from a book, is the priest who won the lawsuit.
Núñez put himself at the funeral he had fought for.
Now look above the row of faces, a little left of centre.
Find a knight with a red cross on his chest, his hand raised.
Just above that hand, one man is not watching the miracle.
He is looking straight at you.
He is said to be El Greco himself.
Now the lower left corner.
A small boy in black, holding a torch.
He points at the saints, and looks out at you.
This is the painter's son, Jorge Manuel.
Look at the white handkerchief in his pocket.
On it El Greco wrote his own name, and the year fifteen seventy-eight.
Not the year of the painting.
The year the boy was born.
El Greco probably never married the boy's mother.
But he signed his greatest picture on his son, and put the child at the front, where no one could miss him.
Lift your eyes.
Up the middle, an angel carries something small and pale, like a newborn baby.
It is the dead man's soul, squeezed upward through a narrow passage of cloud.
Look among the blessed at the top for faces in black.
El Greco even placed the living king of Spain up there.
When it was finished, the valuers named a price.
The parish thought it far too much.
Arguments, appeals, lawyers.
In the end El Greco gave in and accepted the lower valuation, and part of it was paid off against debts he owed.
That was his life in Toledo.
He rented a huge set of rooms in an old palace by the Jewish quarter, more than twenty of them.
He lived grandly.
It is said he sometimes had musicians play while he dined.
And he was always in court, suing patrons who would not pay.
One more glimpse of him.
When a fellow Greek was brought before the Inquisition in Toledo, El Greco was called in to interpret.
A foreigner himself, translating for one of his own, before the most feared court in Spain.
He died in Toledo, still working, with debts unpaid.
On his deathbed he gave his son the power to write his will.
Look back at the boy one last time.
Four hundred years on, he is still pointing, still asking you to look.
Walk on, down the hill, to the great stone monastery with chains on its walls.
That is stop two, San Juan de los Reyes.

tracks.room: Church of Santo Tomé, Calle Santo Tomé

tracks.title: Stop 2. San Juan de los Reyes: A tomb left empty

segments.text: Stop two.
The monastery of San Juan de los Reyes.
Before you go in, stay outside.
Find the long wall of pale stone facing the street, and look up.
Iron chains, hanging in loops high on the stone.
Shackles.
Manacles.
From the street they look like decoration.
They are not.
These chains were worn by Christian prisoners held in the Muslim kingdom of Granada.
As the armies of Isabella and Ferdinand took its towns, one by one, the captives were set free, and their chains were sent here and hung on the wall of the queen's church.
Which prisons, exactly?
The stories differ.
Some say Granada itself.
Others name Málaga, or Ronda, or towns further east.
What they agree on is the message.
Look what we did.
We brought our people home.
You have just come from Granada.
Picture a man stepping out of a cell there, into the light, rubbing his wrists.
His chains ended up here, as a trophy.
Now hold a question as you go in.
Why build a church this grand, and then not use it for the one thing it was made for?
Go back to the beginning.
When Isabella claimed the crown of Castile, her claim was not safe.
Her niece said the crown was hers, and the king of Portugal married that niece and marched into Castile to take it.
In fourteen seventy-six the two armies met near a town called Toro, on the river Duero.
The fighting went on into the dark.
On one side of the field the Portuguese did well.
On the other, Ferdinand's men broke them.
Both sides claimed the victory.
But Isabella understood something.
A battle is won by whoever tells the story.
She called it a triumph, gave thanks, and vowed a monastery.
Here, in Toledo, the old heart of Castile.
And it would be their tomb.
The architect was Juan Guas, the queen's master of works.
Now a story Toledo loves to tell.
The queen came to see how her church was going.
She looked around and asked whether this trifle was what they had built her.
In old Spanish, "esta nonada".
A nothing.
It is a story, and the words differ from one telling to the next.
But the building did change.
It grew richer, and grander, to match her vow.
Walk up to the crossing, where the great stone arches meet.
Look at the walls.
They are covered in coats of arms, held up by huge stone eagles.
The eagle is the sign of Saint John, whose church this is.
Now look for two small emblems, again and again.
A yoke, the wooden collar for oxen.
And a bundle of arrows.
The yoke was Ferdinand's sign.
The arrows were Isabella's.
The popular story says each picked the other's initial.
Yugo, yoke, with a Y, the old spelling of Isabel.
Flechas, arrows, with an F, for Fernando.
Whether or not that is why they chose them, look how they are carved here.
Side by side, again and again, like lovers' initials on a tree.
So why are they not here?
Because of Granada.
In fourteen ninety-two the last Muslim kingdom in Spain surrendered, and the Alhambra was theirs.
The queen loved that city.
She decided to be buried there instead, in the place of her greatest victory.
When she died, her body was carried south and laid first in a convent inside the Alhambra itself.
If you walked past the Parador hotel up there, that old convent is where she first lay.
Later she and Ferdinand were moved to the Royal Chapel, beside Granada's cathedral.
They are there still.
This church was left without its king and queen.
A tomb with nobody in it.
Before you leave, walk into the cloister.
Two floors of arches around a garden.
Look up at the carving, at the beasts and odd creatures sticking out from the walls.
In eighteen hundred and eight, Napoleon's troops occupied Toledo and were quartered here.
A great fire broke out.
The second cloister was destroyed altogether.
Much of what you see was rebuilt later, by restorers working from what survived.
One wing of this cloister and the lace of stone along its top are largely theirs.
So look closely.
Some faces up there were carved five centuries ago.
Some, little more than one.
See if you can tell which.
Stand in the garden.
Think of that wall outside.
The chains of men set free, hung on a church built for a queen who chose to lie somewhere else.
Walk on, uphill, across the old town, to the little mosque of Cristo de la Luz.
That is stop three.

tracks.room: Jewish quarter, Calle de los Reyes Católicos

tracks.title: Stop 3. Cristo de la Luz: The mosque by daylight

segments.text: Stop three.
The little mosque of Cristo de la Luz, near the Sun Gate.
You know its legend already, the king's horse that knelt in the street, and the lamp still burning behind the wall.
Now see the building by daylight.
Start outside, on the street side.
Find the front wall of narrow red bricks, with its three arched doorways.
Above them, blind arches cross and weave like basketwork.
Now look along the very top, just under the roof line.
A band of brick letters runs across it.
That is Arabic, in an old, square, angular script.
And it is a signature.
It says, in short, that a man named Ahmad ibn Hadidi had this mosque built, hoping for his reward from God.
That it was finished, with God's help, under the direction of a builder, Musa ibn Ali, and a man called Saada.
And it gives the date.
The year Christians count as nine hundred and ninety-nine.
Think about that.
One man's money.
One builder's skill.
A small neighbourhood mosque, at the end of the first millennium.
Toledo had many like it.
Almost all are gone.
This is the one that survived, and it still carries the name of the man who made it.
Now go inside.
It is tiny.
Four columns hold up the whole roof.
Stand in the middle, between them.
Look at the tops of the columns, the capitals.
They do not match, and they are rougher than the walls around them.
That is because the builder did not carve them.
He reused them.
They came from older buildings, from the Christian Visigoths who ruled Toledo before the Muslims came.
One was remade in a restoration a century ago.
So the oldest stones holding up this mosque were carved by Christians, and they would hold it up again when it became a church.
Now look up.
The ceiling is divided into nine little squares, three by three.
Each one has its own small dome.
And each dome is made differently.
Brick ribs crossing in a new pattern every time.
Stars.
Crosses.
Grids.
Turn slowly and look at all nine.
It is a builder showing off nine ways to make a sky.
If you saw the great mosque of Córdoba, you will know this family of ribbed domes from the dome in front of its prayer niche.
This is its small country cousin.
Now look east, to the far end.
The style changes.
A rounded apse, a half-circle chamber, joined on in the same red brick, but later.
After the Christian conquest, the mosque passed to a crusading order, the Knights of Saint John, and about two centuries after it was built, they added this apse.
Christian prayer had to face east, so the church grew a new head.
Look into the curved vault of the apse.
Faded paintings, patchy.
At the centre was Christ in majesty, seated in glory.
Much of it has flaked away.
Look for an outline, a hand, a halo.
One building, joined at the seam.
Muslim domes on one side.
Christian saints on the other.
One last thing, outside again.
This hill was a Roman town before it was anything else.
About twenty years ago, archaeologists digging beside the mosque uncovered a stretch of Roman street.
Big granite paving slabs, a road about five metres wide, with a drain running underneath.
Look in the garden area next to the building for the opened ground.
Sources disagree on exactly where it shows, so if you cannot see it, check at the door.
Picture carts rolling over those slabs, nearly a thousand years before the bricks went up.
So stand here for a moment.
Roman stones in the ground.
Visigothic capitals in the columns.
A Muslim builder's name above the door.
Christian saints at the end.
All of Toledo, in a room you could cross in ten steps.
Walk on, through the old streets, to the church of San Román.
That is stop four.

tracks.room: Near Puerta del Sol, Calle Cristo de la Luz

tracks.title: Stop 4. San Román: Arabic on a Christian wall

sections.title: A church that speaks two languages
The victory painted on the walls
The boy king in the tower

segments.text: Stop four.
The church of San Román, on the high ground at the centre of the old town.
These days it is the Museum of the Councils and Visigothic Culture.
Go in, stand in the middle of the nave, and look at the arches first.
Horseshoe arches, in rows, like the ones you just saw at the little mosque.
Now look at the columns holding them up.
They do not match.
Some are older than the church by many centuries, taken from Visigothic and even Roman buildings and set up again here.
But this was never a mosque.
It was built as a church, by Christians, in the Mudéjar way: the building style of Muslim craftsmen, working for Christian patrons.
Hold a question.
Why would a Christian archbishop want Arabic letters in his church?
Here is the scene.
Early in the thirteenth century, a Christian army has just crushed a Muslim army in the south, at a place called Las Navas de Tolosa.
The Archbishop of Toledo rode with that army.
Back home, he has this church painted and consecrated again, to celebrate.
Now look up at the walls.
The paintings are in two bands, one above the other, with a strip of lettering running between them.
Look for the four evangelists, each with wings.
Look for a row of bishops, the archbishops of Toledo.
Look for two young saints in deacon's robes, Stephen and Lawrence.
And look around the arches for more bands of writing.
Some of it is Latin, in verse.
Some of it is in Arabic letters.
One answer to the question: in Toledo, Arabic was not only the enemy's script.
It was the look of beauty and learning, the way fine buildings were dressed.
So a victory over the Muslim south was painted in a style that came from it.
Scholars still argue over what some of that Arabic says, and whether it was meant to be read at all.
Perhaps it was there simply to look splendid.
Now find the Last Judgement.
In Christian belief it is the day the dead rise from their graves to be judged.
See if you can find them, small figures rising to face their judge.
In a church built to give thanks for a battle, the painters put the end of the world.
Everyone, winner and loser, will answer in the end.
Before you go further, a story about the tower outside.
Toledo tells that in a time of civil war, when the city was held by rivals, a child king of Castile was brought in by surprise, and shown to the people from the tower of San Román.
The city rose for him, and his enemies fled.
That boy grew up to be the king who won at Las Navas.
The details vary from one teller to the next.
But it is a good tale to have in your head when you look up at that tower.
Now walk round the cases.
Before the Muslims came, Toledo was the capital of the Visigoths, a Germanic people who ruled Spain from here for well over a century.
Their bishops met in great councils in this city, and at one of them a king gave up his old faith and took the Catholic one.
That is why the museum carries the councils' name.
Look for the belt buckles, the jewellery, the carved stones.
And look for the copies of the gold crowns of Guarrazar.
Check at the door if you cannot find them.
The story goes that one summer in the eighteen fifties, after heavy rain near a village outside Toledo, a farming couple found gold glinting in the earth.
It was a buried hoard of crowns and crosses, hidden, it is thought, when the Muslims arrived.
Pieces were sold off quietly, some to France.
The originals are now in Madrid and Paris.
Kings hung them over altars as gifts to God.
On the finest, gold letters hang from the rim, spelling out a king's name and the words "offers this".
If the copies here include it, find those letters.
One crown, of another king, was stolen from the royal armoury in Madrid in the twentieth century.
It has never been found.
Stand under the arches once more.
Roman columns.
Visigothic gold.
Arabic letters.
Christian saints, and the Last Judgement.
One small church, holding every Toledo at once.
Walk on, downhill, to the cathedral.
That is stop five.

tracks.room: Museum of the Councils and Visigothic Culture, Calle San Román

tracks.title: Stop 6. Toledo: The city of three cultures

segments.text: Stop six, the last.
Play this wherever you are.
If you can, find a spot where you can see the river bending round the rock.
You will hear it everywhere in Toledo.
The city of three cultures.
Christians, Muslims and Jews, side by side.
It is on the posters and in the shops.
Is it true?
The honest answer is yes, and no.
Think of what you saw today.
A mosque whose builder signed his name in brick.
A church with Arabic letters round its arches.
And in the Jewish quarter you walked through, two synagogues still stand, one built by Muslim craftsmen, one decorated like a palace of Granada.
In this city, scholars of three faiths worked together, turning books from Arabic into Latin and Castilian.
Astronomy, medicine, philosophy, much of it Greek learning kept alive in Arabic, came back into Europe through Toledo.
That was real.
It made this city.
But living side by side is not the same as being equal.
Jews and Muslims lived under Christian law, protected in good times, and in bad times by nobody.
In thirteen ninety-one, riots swept the Jewish quarters of Castile.
Synagogues were taken.
Then, fourteen ninety-two.
The year Granada fell.
That spring, Isabella and Ferdinand signed the order expelling every Jew who would not convert.
They signed it in the Alhambra.
The palace you walked through.
Families who had lived here longer than anyone could remember had a few months to go.
Many left, for Portugal, North Africa, the lands of the Ottomans.
Their descendants kept speaking a form of Spanish for five hundred years.
The Muslims of Castile were forced to convert a few years later, and a century after that, their descendants were expelled too.
Some Sephardic families are said to have carried the keys of their Spanish houses with them, and kept them for generations.
It is hard to prove.
The story has never died.
So the three cultures are here, in the stone.
The people who made it are mostly gone.
The beauty is real.
The loss is real.
Toledo asks you to carry both.
Look at the river one last time, wrapped round the city like an arm.
Thank you for walking it with me, Monica.
Take the train back to Madrid.
And if you go back to the Prado, find El Greco again.
You have stood in his city now, in front of his son.
His saints will look different.
Goodbye, Toledo.

tracks.room: Anywhere, ideally a viewpoint over the river

tracks.title: Toledo after dark: the legends

sections.title: A city that keeps its secrets

segments.text: Good evening, Monica.
The sun has gone down behind the river, the day crowds have gone home, and Toledo is starting to change.
You have seen this city by daylight.
Churches, synagogues, a cathedral, the old mosque.
Christians, Jews and Muslims, living side by side on one rock above the Tagus for centuries.
Tonight is for the other Toledo.
The one that people whisper about.
For hundreds of years, all over Europe, this city's name meant magic.
Students were said to come here to learn to raise the dead.
Kings were said to lose their kingdoms here by opening the wrong door.
Statues here move.
Crucifixes speak.
A wooden man once walked these streets.
Why here?
Think about where you are standing.
A maze of lanes too narrow for the moon.
Three faiths, each with its own scholars and its own secrets.
Libraries full of books in languages most of Europe could not read.
A city like that breeds stories after dark.
The Spanish have a phrase for a night when nobody sleeps.
Una noche toledana.
A Toledan night.
One story behind the phrase is the darkest in the city.
Listen.
More than a thousand years ago, Toledo kept rebelling against the emir in far-off Córdoba.
So the emir sent a new governor, a man named Amrus.
He announced a great feast to welcome the prince, and invited the leading men of Toledo to his palace.
They came in, one by one, through a single gate.
And one by one, as they entered, they were killed.
Their bodies went into a pit dug in secret.
Hundreds of them.
Toledo did not sleep that night.
And it did not rebel again for a long time.
Arab chroniclers tell this massacre as history, and some scholars doubt it.
And the phrase may come from something smaller.
An old dictionary from four centuries ago blamed it on the mosquitoes, which ate visitors alive in the summer heat.
At seven, you join the legends tour.
It will be in Spanish.
Each track here tells you one story in English, before you get there.
Listen over a drink, or standing at the place itself.
Then, when the guide stops, drops their voice and points, you will know exactly what they are pointing at.
You will know when the horse kneels, and when the statue moves.
One promise.
When I tell you a legend, you will hear it in another voice.
When I tell you what really happened, it will be me.
Keep them apart, and enjoy both.
Some of the places are shut at night, and you will only see their doors and walls.
That is how legends should be met.
From outside, in the dark.
Start with the little mosque by the old gate, and a horse that would not take another step.
That is stop one.

tracks.room: Anywhere in the old town, before the tour

tracks.title: Stop 1. Cristo de la Luz: the horse that knelt

sections.title: The horse that would not move

segments.text: Stop one.
The small brick mosque of Cristo de la Luz stands on a steep lane just inside the old walls, near the Puerta del Sol gate.
It closes before dark, so tonight you will see it from outside: a little square building of red brick, with arches over arches in its walls.
It is older than almost anything around you.
An inscription on its front gives the year it was finished, nine hundred and ninety-nine.
A thousand years ago, this was a neighbourhood mosque.
Now the story.
Picture a spring day, almost a century later.
Toledo has opened its gates to a Christian king.
King Alfonso rides in at the head of his army, in triumph, up this very slope.
Beside him rides his greatest knight, they say, the Cid.
And then, here, outside this little mosque, the king's horse stops.
It will not go on.
The king spurs it.
Nothing.
And then, in front of the whole army, the horse slowly bends its front legs, and kneels in the street.
Facing the wall of the mosque.
Why would a horse kneel to a wall?
Hold that question.
The king orders the wall opened.
The soldiers strike at the stones.
And behind them they find a hollow, a hidden niche.
Inside it, a crucifix.
And beside the crucifix, an oil lamp.
Still burning.
Here is the secret, as the legend tells it.
Nearly four hundred years before, when the Muslim armies came, the Christians of Toledo hid their Christ in this wall to save it, and lit a lamp beside it.
They sealed it up.
They died.
Nobody remembered.
And all that time, in the dark, the little flame kept burning.
Waiting for someone to come back for it.
That is why the building is called Christ of the Light.
And they say the king held the first Christian Mass here, and left his shield behind, with a cross on it, hanging in the church.
Now the history.
The king was real, and he did take Toledo in ten eighty-five.
The mosque really did become a chapel.
But the legend appears only after the conquest, told by the winners.
Some tellings even forget the lamp.
Others put the Cid on the horse.
The kneeling horse belongs to the story, not the record.
When you are outside, look down at the paving in front of the building.
Toledans say one white stone marks the spot where the horse went down on its knees.
Look for it with the guide's torch.
And stand a moment with this.
The lamp of the legend burned for a faith that was hidden.
The building that kept it was built by another faith.
Whose light is it?
Next, down under the streets near the cathedral, to a palace no king was ever meant to open.
That is stop two.

tracks.room: Mosque of Cristo de la Luz, near the Puerta del Sol gate, north side of the old town

tracks.title: Stop 2. The Cave of Hercules: the king who broke the locks

segments.text: Stop two.
The Cave of Hercules is under a narrow alley called Callejón de San Ginés, a short walk from the cathedral.
It opens only for a few hours in the daytime, so tonight you will stand at a plain door in the alley and look down, in your mind, into the dark.
Long ago, they say, the hero Hercules came to Spain and founded this city.
He was strong, but he was also a magician.
And under this hill he built an enchanted palace.
Inside, he left a secret.
Then he sealed the door with a lock.
Every king who ruled in Toledo after him came here and added one more lock.
Century after century, the door grew heavier with iron.
Until a king came who wanted to know.
What could be worth so many locks?
His name was Rodrigo, the last king of the Goths.
He believed there was treasure inside.
His lords begged him not to.
He broke the locks anyway, one after another, and walked in with a torch.
There was no gold.
There was only a chest.
And in the chest, a folded cloth.
He unfolded it.
Painted on it were horsemen he had never seen.
Strange faces.
Turbans on their heads.
Bows and lances in their hands.
And words beneath them.
Whoever opens this, men like these will take his kingdom.
Imagine him holding that cloth.
The torch shaking.
Every lock on the floor around him, broken by his own hand.
Within a year, the riders came.
They crossed the sea from Africa, and Rodrigo rode out to meet them, and he was never seen again.
The Goths' Spain was gone.
And why did they come?
Toledo has a second story for that.
Go down to the river, by the old bridge of San Martín, and you will find a ruined tower called the Bath of La Cava.
They say that from it, King Rodrigo watched a young girl bathing in the Tagus.
Florinda, the daughter of Count Julian.
He wanted her, and he took her.
Her father, who guarded the strait for the king, swore revenge.
And he opened the way across the sea for the invaders.
Now the history.
Rodrigo was real.
He really was the last Gothic king, and he really did lose his kingdom in battle in seven hundred and eleven.
The locked palace, the painted riders and Florinda are legend, written down by chroniclers long after.
And the cave itself?
Archaeologists say it is a Roman water tank, part of the system that fed the city.
The tower by the river is the stump of a medieval bridge.
Stand at the door and ask yourself the king's question.
Would you have opened it?
Next, the city of magicians, and the man who could make you live a whole life in an afternoon.
That is stop three.

tracks.room: Cueva de Hércules, Callejón de San Ginés, a few minutes from the cathedral

tracks.title: Stop 3. Toledo, school of magic: Don Illán and the Dean

sections.title: The city where they taught the dark arts

segments.text: Stop three.
This story has no single address.
The tour may tell it in a lane near the cathedral, or at the mouth of a cellar.
In the Middle Ages, across Europe, if a man said he had studied in Toledo, people crossed themselves.
The Toledan arts meant necromancy.
Students were said to learn it in caves beneath this city.
Here is the real root of the rumour.
After the Christian conquest, scholars came here from all over Europe.
Toledo had what no one else had: Arabic books on stars, medicine, mathematics, the Greek philosophers.
Christians, Jews and Muslims sat together and turned those books into Latin.
Astronomy looked like sorcery to people who could not read it.
So Toledo became the city of magicians.
A Spanish prince wrote the most famous of these stories seven centuries ago.
Listen.
A churchman, the Dean of Santiago, rides all the way to Toledo.
He has heard of a master of magic, Don Illán.
He begs to be taught.
